# Discussion

## Main findings

This study examined whether exposure to extreme heat around the recommended vaccination date was associated with the timeliness of routine childhood vaccination in Nigeria. Overall, vaccination timeliness was sub-optimal and varied across antigens. BCG and Pentavalent 1 were the only vaccines for which the median age at vaccination fell within the recommended vaccination period, and they also had the highest proportion of children vaccinated within 28 days of the recommended date (53% and 51%, respectively). Timeliness was generally lower for vaccines scheduled later in childhood, with Vitamin A showing the greatest delay and the lowest proportion vaccinated within 28 days (18%). Although vaccination coverage by three years exceeded 50% for all antigens, the relatively low coverage within the 28-day timeliness threshold indicates substantial delays in receiving routine vaccines.

The findings on heat exposure varied according to the measure of heat exposure and antigen. Heatwave exposure was not significantly associated with vaccination timeliness across all antigens while the heat-index exposure showed a more consistent pattern for BCG, Pentavalent 1 and Pentavalent 2, with longer vaccination times under Caution and Extreme Caution conditions compared with Tolerable conditions. These differences were less apparent for the later antigens, for which estimates were generally closer to the null. The model-standardized predictions reflected these patterns, with predicted vaccination coverage within the timeliness thresholds generally higher under Tolerable heat-index conditions for the earlier antigens, while predictions were virtually unchanged between Heatwave and No Heatwave scenarios.

## Vaccine timeliness and heat exposure

In this study, heatwave exposure was not clearly associated with vaccination timeliness. Although the point estimates suggested longer vaccination times for BCG, Pentavalent 1 and Pentavalent 2 among children exposed to heatwaves, the confidence intervals were wide and included the null value of 1 for all antigens. The largest estimate was observed for BCG, with children exposed to a heatwave having an estimated 2.19-fold longer time to vaccination (95% CI: 0.76–6.34), although the considerable uncertainty around this estimate limits the strength of this finding. The relatively small proportion of children exposed to heatwaves may have contributed to the limited precision of these estimates. In contrast, the heat-index analysis showed a more consistent pattern, particularly for vaccines administered earlier in childhood. Compared with Tolerable conditions, both Caution and Extreme Caution conditions were associated with longer estimated vaccination times for BCG, with ETRs of 1.32 (95% CI: 1.11–1.57) and 1.71 (95% CI: 1.34–2.18), respectively, and similar patterns were observed for Pentavalent 1 and Pentavalent 2. The direction of these associations was therefore broadly consistent across the two measures of heat exposure for the earlier antigens, with point estimates above 1 suggesting longer times to vaccination among children exposed to extreme heat. However, the heat-index estimates were more precise, with narrower confidence intervals than those observed for heatwave exposure. This may partly reflect the more balanced distribution of children across the Tolerable, Caution and Extreme Caution categories, which provided more information for comparison than the highly imbalanced Heatwave and No Heatwave groups. The strength of the association also appeared to decrease for vaccines administered later in childhood. For Pentavalent 3, the ETRs were close to 1 under both Caution (1.03) and Extreme Caution (1.06), while the estimates for Vitamin A were slightly below 1 (0.95 for both categories) and those for MCV1 were essentially null (1.00 for Caution and 1.02 for Extreme Caution). Although the direction of the associations was not consistent across all antigens, both heat exposure measures showed larger point estimates for the earlier vaccines, with the associations generally approaching the null value of 1 for vaccines administered later in the immunization schedule.

The lower vaccination timeliness and longer delays observed for Vitamin A compared with MCV1, despite Vitamin A being scheduled earlier in childhood, may partly reflect differences in how the two interventions are delivered. MCV1 is historically well established within routine childhood immunisation services, whereas Vitamin A supplementation relies more heavily on periodic, campaign-based delivery, including the bi-annual Maternal, Newborn and Child Health Weeks (MNCHWs) and National Immunisation Plus Days in Nigeria [@aghaji2019]. The step-like pattern observed in the cumulative Vitamin A vaccination curve provides some support for this explanation, as the increases in coverage appear to occur in distinct periods rather than through the more gradual accumulation observed for the other routine vaccines. This pattern may be consistent with supplementation being delivered during periodic campaigns, resulting in groups of children receiving Vitamin A at similar times rather than continuously according to the recommended age. However, this interpretation should be treated as a possible explanation rather than a direct finding, as the study did not assess the source or mode of delivery of Vitamin A supplementation.

## Model-standardized vaccination timeliness predictions

In the model standardized predictions of vaccination coverage across the timeliness thresholds, the heat-index models showed a consistent pattern for BCG, Pentavalent 1 and Pentavalent 2, with predicted vaccination coverage generally highest under Tolerable conditions and progressively lower under Caution and Extreme Caution conditions. This difference was most apparent for the earlier vaccines and became smaller for vaccines administered later in childhood. For example, at the 28-day threshold, predicted BCG coverage was 39% under Tolerable conditions, compared with 36% under Caution and 33% under Extreme Caution, whereas the differences were much smaller for Pentavalent 3, Vitamin A and MCV1, suggesting that higher levels of heat-index exposure may be more relevant to timely receipt of vaccines administered earlier in the immunization schedule. In contrast, the standardized predictions under the Heatwave and No Heatwave scenarios were virtually identical across all antigens, including at the 28-day threshold, where BCG coverage was 36% under both scenarios and the differences for the other antigens were similarly small. This is consistent with the heatwave AFT estimates, which generally showed wide uncertainty and estimates that approached the null for the later antigens. The progressively smaller differences across heat-index categories for later vaccines may indicate that the influence of heat on vaccination timeliness is less pronounced as children become older. A possible explanation is that vaccination opportunities for older infants may be less closely tied to the immediate environmental conditions around the scheduled vaccination date, but this requires further investigation. The standardized predictions reinforce the pattern observed in the AFT coefficients, that, the differences between heat-index categories were more apparent for earlier vaccines, while vaccination timeliness for later vaccines was relatively similar across heat-exposure scenarios.

## Comparison to other studies

The findings of this study are generally consistent with previous evidence showing that vaccination timeliness tends to decline across the childhood vaccination schedule, although the magnitude of delays differed substantially between studies. In the Ethiopian DHS analysis by Wagner et al. [@wagner2021], the proportion of children vaccinated within 28 days of the recommended date was considerably higher for the pentavalent vaccines than observed in this study, with coverage of 94.7%, 92.8% and 71.7% for Pentavalent 1, Pentavalent 2 and Pentavalent 3, respectively, compared with 51%, 42% and 34% in this study. BCG coverage within 28 days was more similar between the two studies (58.7% vs 53%), while MCV1 coverage was lower in the Ethiopian study (30.6%) than in this study (36%). The median delays were also substantially shorter in the Ethiopian study, ranging from 7 days for BCG and Pentavalent 1 to 45 days for MCV1, compared with 22, 25, 57, 207 and 314 days for BCG, Pentavalent 1, Pentavalent 2, Pentavalent 3 and MCV1, respectively. A similar pattern of increasing delay across the vaccination schedule has been reported across multiple LMIC settings. Using 91 DHS surveys, Clark et al. [@clark2026] reported median delays of 1.0, 1.4, 2.6, 3.9 and 2.2 weeks for BCG, DTP1, DTP2, DTP3 and MCV1, respectively, while 79%, 70%, 59%, 50% and 56% of vaccinations were timely using the same 28-day threshold. These estimates are substantially higher than the corresponding 28-day coverage observed in this study (53%, 51%, 42%, 34% and 36%). Similarly, an analysis of 45 LMIC DHS surveys found median delays of 2.3 weeks for BCG, 2.4 weeks for DTP1, 6.2 weeks for DTP3 and 2.7 weeks for MCV1 [@clark2009]. Evidence from 54 LMICs [@derqui2024], also showed that vaccination timeliness was generally better for birth and earlier doses and declined for later doses, with median delays increasing from 1 week for BCG and DTP1 to 4 weeks for DTP3. The findings from this study are therefore consistent with the broader literature in showing poorer timeliness for vaccines administered later in childhood, but the substantially longer delays and lower 28-day coverage observed in this study suggest that routine vaccination in this Nigerian population may be less timely than that reported across several other LMIC settings, as Nigeria is among the African countries with the lowest vaccine coverage [@simon2025].

The findings on heat exposure are also broadly consistent with the study by Siddiqi et al. [@siddiqi2025], which reported reductions in immunizations administered on days with higher heat-index levels compared with Tolerable conditions. However, the heat-index categories in the present study differed from those used by Siddiqi et al. We classified heat exposure into Tolerable, Caution and Extreme Caution conditions, corresponding to heat-index ranges of \<26.67°C, 26.67–32.22°C and 32.22–39.44°C, respectively, while Siddiqi et al. used the ranges Tolerable (\<33°C), Caution/Extreme Caution, (33–39°C) Danger (40–54°C) and Extreme Danger (\>54°C). The present findings therefore suggest that differences in vaccination timeliness may be observable even at lower levels of heat exposure than those associated with the most extreme heat conditions in Siddiqi et al., although the outcomes are not directly comparable (their study examined the number of immunizations administered on particular days, whereas this study examined vaccination timeliness using the age-at-vaccination). Nevertheless, the broadly similar direction of findings across the two heat measures in the present study, together with the findings reported by Siddiqi et al., provides some evidence that increasing heat exposure may be relevant to routine vaccination delivery and timeliness.

## Strengths and Limitations

The strengths of this study include the use of two established measures of heat exposure, which allowed heat exposure to be assessed from different perspectives. The heatwave measure was location-specific, as heatwaves were defined relative to the usual temperature conditions at each location, while, the heat-index measure used fixed temperature thresholds, allowing the same heat category to have the same meaning across locations. Using both measures therefore allowed the study to assess whether the findings were consistent across different approaches to defining extreme heat. A further strength was the use of a survival modelling framework, which allowed vaccination timing to be analysed while accounting for different levels of vaccination-date information. Children with complete vaccination dates could be included based on their observed vaccination times, while children without a recorded vaccination date could be appropriately treated as censored observations. This allowed more of the available DHS information to be retained than would have been possible using an analysis based only on children with complete vaccination dates. Last, to the best of my knowledge, this is the first study to examine the association between heat exposure and vaccination timeliness using individual-level vaccination data in a cross-sectional population survey. The study therefore provides an initial assessment of whether exposure to extreme heat around the recommended vaccination date may be related to delays in routine childhood vaccination.

This study also has several limitations. First, the observational design and cross-sectional nature of the DHS data do not allow causal conclusions to be drawn from the observed associations. The associations observed in this study should therefore be interpreted as relationships rather than evidence that heat exposure directly causes vaccination delays. Second, the construction of the heatwave exposure involved several methodological decisions. These included the choice of a 5-day rolling average, the length of the historical baseline period (1940–2019), the use of a 4-year return level to define heatwave events, and the 14-day exposure window around the recommended vaccination date. These choices may affect the classification of heatwave exposure. Similarly, the 28-day threshold used to define timely vaccination is a predefined analytical threshold and may not capture all meaningful differences in vaccination timing or be appropriate across all antigens studied. The heat index itself also involves methodological choices, as more than 20 methods have been proposed for its calculation. Although these methods generally produce similar results and are highly correlated, the method used in this study was selected based on the approach recommended by Anderson et al. [@anderson2013]. The resulting heat-index categories were based on established thresholds, but these thresholds may not fully reflect how heat affects populations in the Nigerian context. More broadly, definitions of extreme heat are not completely standardised, and different definitions may produce different estimates of exposure. Third, the heatwave exposure was highly imbalanced, with relatively few children exposed to heatwave conditions compared with those not exposed. This may have reduced the statistical power and precision of the heatwave analyses, as reflected by the relatively wide confidence intervals around some of the estimates. There may also have been residual confounding because some potentially important factors were not available in the DHS data. For example, information on vaccine hesitancy and individual attitudes towards vaccination was not available. The study also did not examine whether the relationship between heat exposure and vaccination timeliness differed according to factors such as travel time to health facilities. Such factors could influence both the likelihood of timely vaccination and the ability of families to seek vaccination during periods of extreme heat.

Another limitation relates to the measurement of vaccination dates in the DHS. Vaccination information may be obtained from vaccination cards or maternal recall which may be subject to recall error. In addition, missing vaccination dates were substantial across the antigens. Although the survival modelling approach allowed children with incomplete vaccination information to be retained through appropriate censoring, missing or inaccurately reported dates may still have affected the estimates of vaccination timeliness. The Weibull distributional assumption used in the accelerated failure time models is another potential limitation. If the distribution of vaccination times does not adequately follow the assumed Weibull form, the estimated associations may not fully represent the underlying relationship between heat exposure and vaccination timing. The study period also included 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic may have disrupted routine immunization services. Such disruptions could have resulted in delays caused by health-system or service-level factors rather than individual decisions to delay vaccination. Although previous studies have reported reductions in routine immunization services during the COVID-19 pandemic [@causey2021; @shet2022], this study did not separately assess or adjust for the potential effects of COVID-19-related disruptions. This may have introduced additional variation in vaccination timeliness that was unrelated to heat exposure. Finally, the number of children eligible for analysis decreased for vaccines administered later in the vaccination schedule. This is partly related to the age range of children included in the DHS and the requirement that children had reached the recommended age for each antigen. The smaller sample sizes for later antigens may have reduced the precision of their estimates and made it more difficult to detect associations between heat exposure and vaccination timeliness. This may be particularly relevant for MCV1, which is scheduled at 9 months and therefore had fewer eligible observations than vaccines administered earlier in childhood.

Future research should examine how different definitions of heat exposure affect estimates of vaccination coverage and timeliness. Combining data from multiple surveys could also allow researchers to examine trends in vaccination timeliness for each antigen over time and assess the effects of health system disruptions, such as those caused by COVID-19, on vaccination timeliness.

## Concluding remarks

This study examined the association between extreme heat exposure and the timeliness of routine childhood vaccination in Nigeria. Overall, vaccination timeliness was sub-optimal, with substantial delays observed across the vaccination schedule. Heatwave exposure was not significantly associated with vaccination timeliness, while, the heat-index analysis showed a more consistent association particularly for vaccines administered earlier in childhood, with longer vaccination times observed under higher heat-index conditions. However, the effect direction was largely consistent across the two heat exposures, with vaccines administered during the early ages being more adversely affected by heat exposure compared to the rest. These findings suggest that the relationship between extreme heat and vaccination timeliness may depend on how heat exposure is defined and may vary across the vaccination schedule. Although the findings do not establish a causal relationship between heat exposure and vaccination delays, they highlight the potential importance of considering extreme heat when planning and delivering routine immunization services. Further research using longitudinal data and alternative definitions of heat exposure is needed to better understand this relationship.
